1: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, I charge thee and I beseech thee, with all the might and all the virtue of my soul, that thou read not this book for curiosity, nor speak of it for chattering, nor teach it out of pride. For only he who is called to be a contemplative can profit by it — and he is called by love, not by learning.

This is the work: that thou lift up thy heart unto the Lord with a meek stirring of love, and mean Him that made thee, and choose Him to be thy God, and keep nothing of the world in thy mind. This work asketh neither long time nor short; for it is ever at hand, as is thy God.

Between thee and thy God there is a cloud of unknowing, and through that cloud thou mayst not pass by thought, nor by imagination, nor by any craft of the mind. But by love it may be pierced, for love is of another manner than knowledge, and it seeth where knowing is blind.
2: [Cloud of Unknowing, ch. 5 — One little word]

And if thou wilt say this little word with thy mouth, or with thy heart, let it be a word of one syllable: GOD. This word is the best of all, for it is the shortest, and it is the ground of all, and in it is all — and a soul that clingeth to it is like a vessel cast upon the sea, where all is deep.

And for to help thee in this work, take good heed that thy mind rest not upon any thought of any thing, whether it be bodily or ghostly. Yea, and in this work thou shalt not think even of God Himself as He is — for that cannot be. Thou shalt think of Him as thou lovest Him; and that is enough.

In the night of this unknowing the soul is like a mirror held up to the sun: it cannot see the sun, but the sun seeth itself in it. And in time the soul is made the mirror of God, and God beholdeth Himself therein, and the soul is made glad with a gladness it cannot name.
3: And if thou wilt be a contemplative, be then a coward of the world's tumult, and flee it as thou wouldst flee the face of a serpent. Not because the world is evil — for God made it and it is good — but because thy work is toward the other side of the cloud, and no man looketh two ways at once.
[Cloud of Unknowing, ch. 42 — The proof of love]

For love may reach to God in this life, but not knowing. And therefore the ghostly work of this book is a reaching and not a seeing; and yet it is more certain than all seeing, for it is the embrace, and the embraced is sure of the embracer.

And if ever thou shalt come to feel Him that thou hast sought, it shall not be as a thing found at last, but as a thing thou never lost — for He was never absent, but only hidden; and the hiding was the cloud, and the cloud is drawn, and there is no more between thee and thy God.
